questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The courses available - I picked Bergen for their courses in Digital Culture. 
The opportunity for guaranteed student housing was also a large factor for me. Similar courses could be found in other universities, so I chose Bergen for the housing advantage.
The natural beauty of the country - exploring Norway was one of the things motivating me for my exchange.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some confusion arose as an exchange student, that the faculty did not seem fully aware of.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Relatively easy, most of it is on the website. 
They also host orientation for new students - I highly recommend coming to these as they function as your guide to campus life.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The aforementioned student orientation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Very easy.
You apply through Sammen for the type of accommodation you want, and they match you with one similar. Exchange students are guaranteed housing. Most are placed at Fantoft Studentboliger, so there is plenty of opportunity for socialising.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Buy the full 6 month public transport pass to save money, you will definitely get your moneys worth. 
Bergen has good public transport, so even if your housing is far away, it should be relatively easy to get to university by the buses or bybanen. 
Make sure to participate in the social events organised by the students - it is here you find most friends in my experience.

Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You are registered through Studentweb, and they run most classes through canvas.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They have exchange coordinators, who are attached to specific faculties. They helped with most questions, especially regarding the OLA.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: 100% successful, as I decided on which classes I wanted to take before I came.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not be afraid to reach out to the exchange coordinators, they are very helpful in my experience.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Interesting lecturers, with varied class activities.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took DIKULT103 and DIKULT104, so entry level courses into the BA in Digital Culture. 
The courses were quite easy to follow as most native Norwegians taking the courses were in their first year of university.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Quite similar. However, there were many more individual assignments and creative projects for students to work creatively on and turn in. These projects were some of the most fun parts of the course. 
The lecturers were very relaxed and personable and appreciated questions a lot. The course was mainly lectures, so no real classroom settings, however, most lecturers used discussion questions multiple times per lecture to activate the students.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
DIKULT103. Digital Aesthetics: art, narrative, and games. 

DIKULT104. Digital Technology and Society.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Both DIKULT103 and DIKULT104 are courses well-suited to humanities students with an interest in the internet, gaming, and computing's impact on art as well as the way humans process these new technologies. We also touched on topics such as AI, DEI in tech, and Digital Art. 
These are not programming courses, though we did do a small module using BASIC.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The cost of fresh fruit and vegetables is quite high in Norway - using frozen alternatives were quite necessary. For instance, a cucumber in some shops would cost around 25 DKK. 
The Erasmus Student Network arranges trips around Norway, which were an expense I had not budgeted for, so I did not participate in them.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Fresh fruit and vegetables, as previously stated. However, most other food items are priced relatively similar to Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
UiB has thousands of student clubs, everything from football to choir singing to anime club. Also, a course to learn Norwegian is offered through UiB. 
My faculty had the Ad Fontes student pub, which was great to hang out in.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking the mountains of Bergen - I waited until the weather was better, but they offer the best views of the city, and some of my favourite memories of Norway are found on its mountains. Bergen has 7 city mountains, most with well marked trails to follow. Particularly Løvstakken is a fun, if challenging, hike.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I travelled to Stavanger and Oslo with friends on weekend trips. Both places are highly recommended, as they are relatively easy to get to, and they offer amazing views along the way. 
From Bergen to Stavanger you can take a ferry through the fjords.
From Bergen to Oslo you can fly, or take a train through beautiful landscape. 
The views on these routes alone made the trips worth it. 
I also took a day trip from Bergen to Flåm, which was also a highlight of my exchange.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy since I share some cultural similarities already, however, I was mostly surrounded by other international students. This is an unintended side effect of the housing guarantee offered by Sammen.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Joining local student clubs. Sitting next to Norwegian students in class and striking up a conversation.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Most Norwegians seem very quiet and reserved when you meet them. (Even more than other Scandinavians.) It can feel like they are uninterested in talking/friendship, but its it more that it takes more time to get through to them.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The focus on using and enjoying nature. Everyone seems to hike, run, or go out to their family cabins to decompress. 
The teaching style being personable. 
The pride they take in their traditions and history, particularly as seen through the public celebrations on the 17th of May.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get used to the rain/snow - I wasted some time waiting for the weather to clear to go on activities. It's better just to have the gear at hand, so you can appreciate the nature comfortably. 

Bergen has a rich cultural life - particularly if you're interested in poetry, literature and art. Check out local groups and poetry readings, as well as the major KODE museums if you're interested. 

Make sure to also go outside Bergen if you can - the outside suburbs as well as other cities entirely have their own charm.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: At the start of each new semester, Sammen holds a free student recycling festival, where you can pick up old items that previous students donated at no cost. Arrive early, and you might be able to furnish all your bedding and household needs without a trip to Ikea.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The projects of my course being satisfying to complete. 
Exploring Stavanger, Oslo, Flåm, Bergen. 
Climbing the mountains and finally reaching the peak after a hard trek. 
Making good friends and telling stories of our lives back home.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: When I first arrived, feelings of nervousness and isolation. However, once you make your first friends, those tend to go away. Erasmus events can be very helpful to make some.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I worked part time as a server in function rooms - this can also be a fun way to interact with native Norwegians of an older generation as well as make some money to go on fun activities. Just make sure to get your D-number at the tax office (Skatteetaten) through your employrer.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
